title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6715 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

For now the signal points the other way: diesel exports are falling and November tracking is weaker. The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts. When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET). Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on). As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

title: Could the internet go dark?
body: Chimpanzees can choose the right tool for a task and even modify it in advance; crows drop stones into water to raise its level and reach floating food; and octopuses can unscrew jars to get to what's inside. That is called causal reasoning, something humans are particularly good at, although it can sometimes lead us down the wrong path. For example, following recent outages in Microsoft services and a technical glitch in the U.S. air traffic control system, some interpreted these as signs of an impending digital apocalypse. There's even a date — November 17th. The theory goes that hackers will break into the world's biggest banks, wipe out everyone's accounts, and shut down the internet for three months, sending the world into chaos and panic. Such fears could also spill over into financial markets, affecting investor confidence and driving demand for safe-haven assets, while putting the U.S. dollar index in focus. The good news is that there's no master switch to turn off the internet. It's a huge network of undersea cables, satellites, data centers, and telecom operators, so taking the whole thing offline is unlikely. Still, the global network does face real threats, just not the kind these theories suggest. A much more likely scenario is a major outage caused by shared dependencies, when multiple services suddenly lose access to the same cloud provider. And we have seen this happen more than once in recent years.

title: Kuroda, once Japan's great easer, says BOJ rates may need to rise above neutral
body: For Japanese rates and the yen, a call for above-neutral rates from the architect of Japan's easing era adds weight to the hawkish tail of BOJ pricing. Most economists see a terminal rate near 1.75%, and talk of 2.5% now has a high-profile backer. Kuroda no longer sets policy, so the direct effect is limited. Still, his critique of the food tax cut puts the fiscal-monetary tension in sharp relief ahead of an expected December hike. Front-end JGB yields, with the two-year near 1.88%, are most exposed to any shift toward a higher peak. Oil matters here too. Kuroda explicitly links Japan's inflation risk to the Iran war, so a renewed energy spike would strengthen the case he describes. --- The governor who took Japan into negative rates now says the BOJ may need to go beyond neutral. He blames imported inflation from the Iran war and a food tax cut he says will feed prices, not growth. Summary: Former BOJ Governor Haruhiko Kuroda says rates may need to rise above neutral if inflation becomes more serious. He cited cost pressures from the US war with Iran, given Japan's reliance on imported oil, materials and food. The BOJ is widely expected to hike next month. Economists see a peak of 1.75%, and some see as high as 2.5%. Kuroda said PM Takaichi's planned food sales tax cut, worth about ¥10 trillion, would push up prices, not growth. He described Japan's July to September contraction as probably temporary.
